Comply outperforms FlyVec on most semantic similarity tasks and is competitive with BERT despite having fewer parameters.
Comply shows more regular and concave performance with respect to hash length k, plateauing at around k=150.
In reinforcement learning, Comply outperforms a Transformer baseline and continues to improve, while P-FlyVec fails to improve.
Comply produces sparse binary hashes that are interpretable, with neurons memorizing contextually relevant short sequences.
The method is computationally efficient, with faster evaluation times than BERT on most tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited to pretraining on large general-purpose corpora and not including sequence similarity objective like sentence Transformers.
Word repetition is supported in a limited way (phases of repeated words are averaged).
future_direction: Including sequence similarity objective as in sentence Transformers.
Extending evaluation to different modalities (e.g., different RL environments or time-series tasks).
Making the model generative for sequence generation.
papers.abstract: Biologically inspired neural networks offer alternative avenues to model data distributions. FlyVec is a recent example that draws inspiration from the fruit fly's olfactory circuit to tackle the task of learning word embeddings. Surprisingly, this model performs competitively even against deep learning approaches specifically designed to encode text, and it does so with the highest degree of computational efficiency. We pose the question of whether this performance can be improved further. For this, we introduce Comply. By incorporating positional information through complex weights, we enable a single-layer neural network to learn sequence representations. Our experiments show that Comply not only supersedes FlyVec but also performs on par with significantly larger state-of-the-art models. We achieve this without additional parameters. Comply yields sparse contextual representations of sentences that can be interpreted explicitly from the neuron weights.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: CAST: Compositional Analysis via Spectral Tracking for Understanding Transformer Layer Functions
papers.research_question: How do transformer layers process information and what are their computational roles? The paper investigates internal mechanisms of transformers through transformation-centric analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CAST, a probe-free framework for analyzing transformer layer functions via direct transformation matrix estimation and spectral analysis, revealing distinct architectural patterns between encoder and decoder models.
papers.conclusion: CAST provides transformation-centric insights into transformer layer functions, revealing architectural patterns and offering practical guidance for model design, pruning, and training optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Decoder-only models (GPT-2, Llama, DeepSeek-R1) exhibit compression-expansion cycles through their layers, with effective rank dropping at middle layers before recovering.
Encoder-only models (RoBERTa) maintain high effective rank throughout their depth, preserving comprehensive representations.
Kernel analysis (CKA) partitions layers into three functional phases: feature extraction, compression, and specialization.
Middle compression layers in decoders exhibit the strongest nonlinearity, suggesting complex transformations during abstraction.
The linear approximation captures substantial transformation behavior, as validated by residual norm analysis.
papers.limitation:
The linear approximation may not capture all nonlinear dynamics of transformer layers.
The analysis is limited to four representative architectures; generalizability to emerging transformer variants requires further investigation.
Spectral analysis provides insights into transformation structure but does not directly address semantic interpretability of the identified patterns.
future_direction: Extending CAST to emerging transformer variants and next-generation architectures.
Integrating spectral analysis with existing probing and visualization techniques for semantic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable success but remain largely black boxes with poorly understood internal mechanisms. To address this limitation, many researchers have proposed various interpretability methods including mechanistic analysis, probing classifiers, and activation visualization, each providing valuable insights from different perspectives. Building upon this rich landscape of complementary approaches, we introduce CAST (Compositional Analysis via Spectral Tracking), a probe-free framework that contributes a novel perspective by analyzing transformer layer functions through direct transformation matrix estimation and comprehensive spectral analysis. CAST offers complementary insights to existing methods by estimating the realized transformation matrices for each layer using Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse and applying spectral analysis with six interpretable metrics characterizing layer behavior. Our analysis reveals distinct behaviors between encoder-only and decoder-only models, with decoder models exhibiting compression-expansion cycles while encoder models maintain consistent high-rank processing. Kernel analysis further demonstrates functional relationship patterns between layers, with CKA similarity matrices clearly partitioning layers into three phases: feature extraction, compression, and specialization.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability (MI) for transformer-based language models, organizing the field from a task-centric perspective and presenting a beginner's roadmap to guide newcomers.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes the current state of mechanistic interpretability for transformer-based LMs, highlights existing challenges, and outlines promising future research directions to advance the field.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability research can be organized around three fundamental objects of study: features, circuits, and universality.
The field has developed a variety of techniques, including vocabulary projection, intervention-based methods, and sparse autoencoders, each with distinct advantages and limitations.
MI has yielded insights into model capabilities such as in-context learning, reasoning, and knowledge mechanisms, and has applications in model enhancement and AI safety.
Current challenges include the scalability of techniques, the need for standardized benchmarks, and the practical utility of MI findings.
Future directions include advancing MI techniques, improving automated hypothesis generation, and exploring new paradigms of human-AI collaboration.
future_direction: Advancement in MI techniques to improve scalability and generalizability.
Development of standardized benchmarks and metrics for evaluating interpretability methods.
Exploration of automated hypothesis generation and new paradigms of human-AI collaboration driven by MI.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is an emerging sub-field of interpretability that seeks to understand a neural network model by reverse-engineering its internal computations. Recently, MI has garnered significant attention for interpreting transformer-based language models (LMs), resulting in many novel insights yet introducing new challenges. However, there has not been work that comprehensively reviews these insights and challenges, particularly as a guide for newcomers to this field. To fill this gap, we provide a comprehensive survey from a task-centric perspective, organizing the taxonomy of MI research around specific research questions or tasks. We outline the fundamental objects of study in MI, along with the techniques, evaluation methods, and key findings for each task in the taxonomy. In particular, we present a task-centric taxonomy as a roadmap for beginners to navigate the field by helping them quickly identify impactful problems in which they are most interested and leverage MI for their benefit. Finally, we discuss the current gaps in the field and suggest potential future directions for MI research.

papers.title: ExPe: Exact Positional Encodings for Generative Transformer Models with Extrapolating Capabilities
papers.research_question: How can we design positional encodings for transformers that enable extrapolation to sequences longer than those seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Exact Positional Encodings (ExPE) and ExQPE, which override specific dimensions of embedding vectors with exact positional information, enabling extrapolation to longer sequences without additional training.
papers.conclusion: ExPE and ExQPE present a promising alternative to existing positional encoding techniques, offering improved extrapolation capabilities and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
ExPE and ExQPE reduce perplexity on sequences longer than training length compared to RoPE and sinusoidal embeddings.
ExPE and ExQPE maintain performance on standard benchmarks (HellaSwag, MMLU, ARC) comparable to RoPE.
ExPE and ExQPE are computationally efficient, requiring less training time and memory than RoPE.
Scaling the encoding values without additional training can further enhance length extrapolation.
papers.limitation:
The models trained are too small and were trained on too short a context length, limiting the generalizability of the results.
The models have not undergone instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning, DPO, or RLHF.
Human language is inherently local, so long dependencies are rare in training data, which may limit the need for long-context models.
future_direction: Conduct larger experiments with more extensive models, greater data, and longer context lengths.
Develop proper benchmarks and training data tailored explicitly to long context dependencies.
Compare the method to techniques like Dual Chunk Attention and Position Interpolation.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to position embeddings in transformer models, named "Exact Positional Embeddings" (ExPE). An absolute positional embedding method that can extrapolate to sequences of lengths longer than the ones it was trained on. Traditional transformer models rely on absolute or relative position embeddings to incorporate positional information into token embeddings, which often struggle with extrapolation to sequences longer than those seen during training. Our proposed method utilizes a novel embedding strategy that encodes exact positional information by overriding specific dimensions of the embedding vectors, thereby enabling a more precise representation of token positions. The proposed approach not only maintains the integrity of the original embeddings but also enhances the model's ability to generalize to more extended sequences. In causal language modeling, our ExPE embeddings significantly reduce perplexity compared to rotary and sinusoidal embeddings, when tested on sequences longer than those used in training.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Amortized Spectral Kernel Discovery via Prior-Data Fitted Network
papers.research_question: How can we extract explicit spectral densities and stationary kernels from pre-trained Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) to improve interpretability and enable downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework and decoder architectures to extract explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels from the latent representations of frozen Prior-Data Fitted Networks, enabling amortized kernel discovery without iterative optimization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that PFNs implicitly encode structured spectral information, which can be decoded into explicit, portable kernel representations, bridging the gap between amortized inference and interpretable kernel discovery for scientific and downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic analysis shows the attention latent output (H) in PFNs encodes the spectral content of the input function, forming a smooth manifold correlated with frequency.
The proposed Filter Bank Decoder can recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and construct explicit stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem.
Decoded kernels achieve Gaussian process regression performance comparable to the original PFN and optimization-based baselines (Deep Kernel Learning, Random Fourier Features) while requiring only a single forward pass, yielding orders-of-magnitude inference speedups.
Theoretical analysis characterizes the identifiability limits of spectral density: spectral weights are non-identifiable from a single normalized realization but become identifiable with multiple independent realizations.
The framework operates effectively in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, with an analytical scaling module to resolve global scale ambiguity in the single-function setting.
papers.limitation:
The decoded kernels are explicit stationary surrogate kernels obtained via Bochner's theorem; they are not exact reconstructions of the PFN's internal attention mechanism nor guaranteed to match the true data-generating GP kernel.
In the single-realization setting, spectral weights are not identifiable from a single normalized function sample, limiting full spectral recovery.
papers.abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) enable efficient amortized inference but lack transparent access to their learned priors and kernels. This opacity hinders their use in downstream tasks, such as surrogate-based optimization, that require explicit covariance models. We introduce an interpretability-driven framework for amortized spectral discovery from pre-trained PFNs with decoupled attention. We perform a mechanistic analysis on a trained PFN that identifies attention latent output as the key intermediary, linking observed function data to spectral structure. Building on this insight, we propose decoder architectures that map PFN latents to explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem. We study this pipeline in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, contextualizing theoretical limits on spectral identifiability and proving consistency when multiple function samples are available. Empirically, the proposed decoders recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and produce explicit kernels that support Gaussian process regression with accuracy comparable to PFNs and optimization-based baselines, while requiring only a single forward pass. This yields orders-of-magnitude reductions in inference time compared to optimization-based baselines.

papers.title: CoPE: A Lightweight Complex Positional Encoding
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to enhance positional encoding in transformers by leveraging complex-valued encoding to separately capture semantic content and positional information.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoPE, a lightweight complex positional encoding that uses phase-aware attention to separate semantic and positional information, avoids long-term decay, is compatible with linear attention, and achieves superior performance on GLUE benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CoPE is a novel positional encoding that encodes context and position through real and imaginary components, demonstrating effectiveness in capturing positional dependencies with computational efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
CoPE does not exhibit long-term decay in attention scores.
CoPE is compatible with linear attention mechanisms.
CoPE achieves lower training loss and better test performance on some GLUE datasets compared to RoPE, Sinusoidal, and Learned encodings.
CoPE has lower computational complexity than RoPE.
Phase-aware attention in the first layer effectively captures positional dependencies.
papers.limitation:
Extrapolation: sinusoidal embeddings may underperform when extrapolated beyond trained sequence length.
Evaluation is limited to smaller models trained from scratch due to resource constraints, not on pretraining or fine-tuning tasks with larger models.
future_direction: Extrapolation experiments with CoPE
Evaluation on pretraining and fine-tuning tasks with larger models
Applications to diverse sequence modeling tasks
papers.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of position encoding in transformer architectures. By incorporating positional information, this approach provides essential guidance for modeling dependencies between elements across different sequence positions. We introduce CoPE (a lightweight Complex Positional Encoding), a novel architecture that leverages complex-valued encoding to encode both content and positional information. Our approach replaces traditional positional encodings with complex embeddings where the real part captures semantic content and the imaginary part encodes positional information. We introduce phase-aware attention in the first layer of the transformer model to capture position-dependent patterns, followed by standard attention layers for higher-levels. We show that CoPE doesn't exhibit long term decay and is compatible with linear attention. Experimental evaluation on the GLUE benchmark suggest that our approach achieves superior performance with less computational complexity, compared to RoPE, Sinusoidal and Learned positional encodings.

papers.title: In-Context Learning Without Copying
papers.research_question: Are induction heads a necessary building block for learning abstractive in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, or can such capabilities emerge independently?
papers.core_contribution: Abstractive in-context learning capabilities can emerge independently of induction heads, as demonstrated by the HAPAX training regime which suppresses inductive copying but preserves abstractive ICL performance.
papers.conclusion: The developmental link between induction heads and abstractive in-context learning capabilities is weaker than previously hypothesized.
papers.key_findings:
HAPAX training reduces inductive copying by 66% on random repetition tasks.
Abstractive ICL capabilities are preserved under HAPAX, with the model achieving higher accuracy on 13 out of 21 tasks.
Models trained with HAPAX develop fewer and weaker induction heads.
The token-loss difference metric is primarily affected by exact copying and does not correlate well with abstractive ICL capabilities.
Previous token heads can lead to prefix-matching patterns even in randomly initialized attention heads.
papers.abstract: Induction heads are attention heads that perform inductive copying by matching patterns from earlier context and copying their continuations verbatim. As models develop induction heads, they experience a sharp drop in training loss, a phenomenon cited as evidence that induction heads may underlie a wide range of in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. In this work, we investigate whether induction heads are a necessary building block for learning abstractive ICL capabilities (i.e., tasks where the answer is not contained in the input context), or whether such capabilities can emerge independently. We propose Hapax, a training regime that omits the loss contribution of tokens predictable by induction heads. Despite a significant reduction in inductive copying, abstractive ICL capabilities are preserved, with the model achieving higher accuracy than the vanilla model on 13 out of 21 tasks, even though 31.7% of tokens are omitted from the loss. Furthermore, our model achieves lower loss values on token positions that induction heads cannot predict. Mechanistic analysis shows that models trained with Hapax develop fewer and weaker induction heads despite preserving abstractive ICL capabilities. Our findings suggest that the developmental link between induction heads and abstractive ICL capabilities is weaker than previously hypothesized.

papers.title: Pretrained Transformers as Universal Computation Engines
papers.research_question: We investigate the capability of a transformer pretrained on natural language to generalize to other modalities with minimal finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: A transformer pretrained on natural language can be effectively transferred to non-language tasks by freezing the self-attention and feedforward layers and only finetuning a small set of parameters, achieving strong performance.
papers.conclusion: Language-pretrained transformers can serve as universal computation engines, transferring effectively to non-language tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT) achieves comparable performance to fully trained transformers on a variety of non-language tasks.
Language pretraining improves performance and compute efficiency over random initialization.
The transformer architecture (even randomly initialized) outperforms LSTM architectures on these tasks.
FPT converges faster than randomly initialized transformers.
The frozen attention layers learn to attend to semantically meaningful patterns in the data (e.g., in bit tasks).
future_direction: Investigating how to increase model expressiveness for better performance.
Exploring multimodal training/architectures.
Studying the role of different pretraining objectives and datasets.
papers.abstract: We investigate the capability of a transformer pretrained on natural language to generalize to other modalities with minimal finetuning -- in particular, without finetuning of the self-attention and feedforward layers of the residual blocks. We consider such a model, which we call a Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT), and study finetuning it on a variety of sequence classification tasks spanning numerical computation, vision, and protein fold prediction. In contrast to prior works which investigate finetuning on the same modality as the pretraining dataset, we show that pretraining on natural language can improve performance and compute efficiency on non-language downstream tasks. Additionally, we perform an analysis of the architecture, comparing the performance of a random initialized transformer to a random LSTM. Combining the two insights, we find language-pretrained transformers can obtain strong performance on a variety of non-language tasks.

papers.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is in-context learning (ICL) in transformers a persistent phenomenon, or does it emerge and then disappear (become transient) during training?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning (ICL) in transformers is often transient: it emerges and then disappears during training, even as training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for in-weights learning (IWL).
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is often transient, emphasizing the importance of validation metrics, early stopping, or regularization to preserve ICL capabilities during training.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges and then disappears (is transient) during training, while IWL accuracy increases.
ICL transience occurs across a range of model sizes (depth, embedding dimension), dataset sizes (number of classes, exemplars per class), and dataset types (Omniglot images, LLaMa token embeddings).
Data distributional properties, such as a larger number of classes or a Zipfian skew, can postpone the transience of ICL.
L2 regularization can mitigate or eliminate ICL transience, potentially by favoring the lower-norm ICL circuit.
Preliminary evidence suggests ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits for resources in the transformer's residual stream.
future_direction: Explore the effect of alternate optimizers or initialization schemes on the transience of ICL.
Connect findings to natural language settings and large-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to "overtrain" transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Low-$N$ Protein Function Prediction and Design
papers.research_question: How effective are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for protein function prediction and design in low-data (low-N) regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a compact and biologically meaningful latent space that improves low-N fitness prediction and enables effective protein design via latent steering, outperforming ESM2 baselines.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a powerful tool for low-N protein function prediction and design, expanding the biologist's toolkit for resource-constrained applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform ESM2 baselines in 58% of fitness extrapolation tasks with as few as 24 training sequences.
SAEs design top-fitness variants in 83% of cases via latent steering, compared to designing with ESM2 alone.
The sparse latent space of SAEs encodes biologically interpretable motifs and compresses relevant information, reducing overfitting in low-N regimes.
Analysis of steered variants reveals that SAEs activate latents corresponding to known biological motifs such as active sites, allosteric sites, and epistatic sites.
SAE performance is influenced by the number of available multiple sequence alignment (MSA) sequences for training.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a set of proteins; it could be extended to other proteins with clinically relevant functions such as antibiotic resistance and viral replication.
SAE performance is strongly influenced by the number of MSA sequences available for training; strategies are needed for robust training when MSAs are shallow.
Protein engineering experiments rely on in-silico fitness models; wet lab validation is necessary to verify function.
Designed variants are constrained to a maximum of five mutations away from the wildtype; beyond this radius, designing highly-functional sequences is difficult with a single predictive latent.
In-silico evaluation tools become less reliable the further away variants are from the wildtype.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other proteins with clinically relevant functions.
Explore strategies for robust SAE training when multiple sequence alignments are shallow or unavailable.
Couple SAE steering with physics-based tools like Rosetta to jointly optimize for both function and stability.
papers.abstract: Predicting protein function from amino acid sequence remains a central challenge in data-scarce (low-$N$) regimes, limiting machine learning-guided protein design when only small amounts of assay-labeled sequence-function data are available. Protein language models (pLMs) have advanced the field by providing evolutionary-informed embeddings and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled decomposition of these embeddings into interpretable latent variables that capture structural and functional features. However, the effectiveness of SAEs for low-$N$ function prediction and protein design has not been systematically studied. Herein, we evaluate SAEs trained on fine-tuned ESM2 embeddings across diverse fitness extrapolation and protein engineering tasks. We show that SAEs, with as few as 24 sequences, consistently outperform or compete with their ESM2 baselines in fitness prediction, indicating that their sparse latent space encodes compact and biologically meaningful representations that generalize more effectively from limited data. Moreover, steering predictive latents exploits biological motifs in pLM representations, yielding top-fitness variants in 83% of cases compared to designing with ESM2 alone.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Beyond Human-Like Processing: Large Language Models Perform Equivalently on Forward and Backward Scientific Text
papers.research_question: Does the success of large language models arise from their flexibility as general pattern learners, rather than from human-like language processing mechanisms? This is investigated by training LLMs on forward and backward scientific text.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer-based LLMs perform equally well on forward and backward scientific text, suggesting they are general pattern learning machines rather than models of human language processing.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based language models are best understood as general pattern learning machines capable of extracting predictive structure from any sufficiently structured input, rather than as specific models of human language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Backward-trained GPT-2 models performed non-significantly better than forward-trained models on the BrainBench task.
Both forward and backward-trained models matched or exceeded human expert performance as model size increased.
Backward-trained models exhibited consistently higher perplexities on validation and test data.
Backward-trained models showed lower correlation with human judgments compared to forward-trained models.
Model judgments correlated more strongly with each other than with human judgments.
papers.abstract: The impressive performance of large language models (LLMs) has led to their consideration as models of human language processing. Instead, we suggest that the success of LLMs arises from the flexibility of the transformer learning architecture. To evaluate this conjecture, we trained LLMs on scientific texts that were either in a forward or backward format. Despite backward text being inconsistent with the structure of human languages, we found that LLMs performed equally well in either format on a neuroscience benchmark, eclipsing human expert performance for both forward and backward orders. Our results are consistent with the success of transformers across diverse domains, such as weather prediction and protein design. This widespread success is attributable to LLM's ability to extract predictive patterns from any sufficiently structured input. Given their generality, we suggest caution in interpreting LLM's success in linguistic tasks as evidence for human-like mechanisms.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Interpreting Evo 2: Arc Institute's Next-Generation Genomic Foundation Model
papers.research_question: How can interpretability techniques be applied to the Evo 2 genomic foundation model to extract biologically relevant features and enable steering for DNA sequence generation?
papers.core_contribution: Applied interpretability techniques to Evo 2 to extract biologically relevant features and demonstrated potential for steering DNA sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability methods applied to Evo 2 reveal biological knowledge and open possibilities for genome engineering and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered features corresponding to biological concepts like coding sequences, protein secondary structure, tRNA/rRNAs, and viral derived sequences.
Validated feature relevance with domain-F1 score alignment analysis.
Found that layer 26 (StripedHyena layer) had the most interesting biologically-relevant features.
Early indications that steering through features could enable controlled DNA sequence generation.
BatchTopK SAEs performed better than standard ReLU SAEs in training loss and feature crispness.
papers.limitation:
Steering is more complex than for language models and requires further research
Work is in early stages
future_direction: Publishing a comprehensive study on interpretability methodology
Unlocking steering capabilities for DNA sequence generation
papers.abstract: How can interpretability techniques be applied to the Evo 2 genomic foundation model to extract biologically relevant features and enable steering for DNA sequence generation? Applied interpretability techniques to Evo 2 to extract biologically relevant features and demonstrated potential for steering DNA sequence generation. Interpretability methods applied to Evo 2 reveal biological knowledge and open possibilities for genome engineering and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Beyond performance: How design choices shape chemical language models
papers.research_question: How do design choices (molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, model architecture) influence the performance and chemical interpretability of chemical language models?
papers.core_contribution: Design choices, particularly molecular representation and tokenization, significantly affect the chemical interpretability of language models, with SMILES and atomwise tokenization yielding more chemically meaningful embeddings, even when downstream task performance is similar.
papers.conclusion: Design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented in language models, and SMILES with atomwise tokenization is favorable for interpretability, guiding future development of chemically grounded CLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Atomwise tokenization generally yields better downstream performance than SentencePiece tokenization.
SMILES representations produce more chemically structured latent spaces than SELFIES representations.
BART and RoBERTa architectures yield comparably interpretable representations, but BART embeddings are more linearly separable for certain molecular properties.
RoBERTa shows a stronger ability to distinguish between atom types than BART.
The choice of molecular representation has a greater impact on interpretability than the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring alternative molecular representations such as t-SMILES and DeepSMILES.
Comparing BART's generative capabilities with other large language model architectures like GPT.
Investigating the differences and synergies between large language models and graph-based approaches such as GROVER.
Utilizing highly curated datasets from specialized domains to reveal subtle chemical relationships.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical language models (CLMs) have shown strong performance in molecular property prediction and generation tasks. However, the impact of design choices, such as molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, and model architecture, on both performance and chemical interpretability remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate how these factors influence CLM performance and chemical understanding. We evaluated models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks and probing the structure of their latent spaces using simple classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques.Despite similar performance on downstream tasks across model configurations, we observed substantial differences in the structure and interpretability of their internal representations. SMILES molecular representation format with atomwise tokenization strategy consistently produced more chemically meaningful embeddings, while models based on BART and RoBERTa architectures yielded comparably interpretable representations. These findings highlight that design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented, even when external metrics appear unchanged. This insight can inform future model development, encouraging more chemically grounded and interpretable CLMs.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Analyzing Encoded Concepts in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether transformer language models encode linguistic concepts in their representations, which concepts dominate the overall structure, and whether the models learn novel concepts beyond linguistic properties.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ConceptX, a framework that uses unsupervised clustering to discover latent concepts in transformer language model representations and aligns them with human-defined concepts to explain how linguistic knowledge is structured across layers and models.
papers.conclusion: ConceptX provides a framework for analyzing encoded concepts in deep NLP models, revealing how linguistic information is structured across layers and highlighting differences between models, with many concepts being compositional or novel.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of transformer models predominantly capture shallow lexical concepts (e.g., ngrams, suffixes), while middle and higher layers better represent core linguistic concepts (e.g., morphology, syntax, semantics).
Multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R) show higher alignment with human-defined concepts compared to monolingual models, likely due to more complex training tasks.
Roughly 50% of the encoded concepts discovered align with the suite of human-defined linguistic concepts; the remaining concepts are novel or compositional, involving multiple fine-grained categories.
The extent of alignment varies across different transformer models and different human-defined concepts, influenced by factors like architecture, training data, and objective function.
Models learn multi-faceted concepts that cannot be adequately explained by existing human-defined concepts, indicating the presence of novel semantic relationships.
papers.limitation:
Clustering a large number of high-dimensional vectors is computationally and memory intensive, requiring the use of a subset of data and limiting the number of tokens per word.
The number of clusters (K=1000) was selected empirically rather than through a rigorous optimization method.
papers.abstract: We propose a novel framework ConceptX, to analyze how latent concepts are encoded in representations learned within pre-trained language models. It uses clustering to discover the encoded concepts and explains them by aligning with a large set of human-defined concepts. Our analysis on seven transformer language models reveal interesting insights: i) the latent space within the learned representations overlap with different linguistic concepts to a varying degree, ii) the lower layers in the model are dominated by lexical concepts (e.g., affixation), whereas the core-linguistic concepts (e.g., morphological or syntactic relations) are better represented in the middle and higher layers, iii) some encoded concepts are multi-faceted and cannot be adequately explained using the existing human-defined concepts.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Is attention required for ICL? Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between model architecture and in-context learning ability? Which architectures are capable of ICL and which exhibit superior performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that in-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with some attention alternatives being competitive with or better than transformers in certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with attention alternatives being competitive. However, no architecture is consistent across all tasks, and performance degrades with out-of-distribution prompt lengths.
papers.key_findings:
All considered architectures can perform in-context learning, demonstrating ICL is not exclusive to attention-based models.
Attention alternatives such as Mamba, Hyena, RetNet, and RWKV are sometimes competitive with or better than transformers at ICL.
Performance varies with number of in-context examples; some architectures show degradation when extrapolating to longer prompts than seen in training.
The emergence of ICL in image classification is influenced by burstiness in training data; some architectures are predisposed towards memorization over ICL.
ICL score in language modeling correlates with performance on other ICL tasks, but not perfectly.
papers.abstract: What is the relationship between model architecture and the ability to perform in-context learning? In this empirical study, we take the first steps toward answering this question. We evaluate thirteen model architectures capable of causal language modeling across a suite of synthetic in-context learning tasks. These selected architectures represent a broad range of paradigms, including recurrent and convolution-based neural networks, transformers, state space model inspired, and other emerging attention alternatives. We discover that all the considered architectures can perform in-context learning under a wider range of conditions than previously documented. Additionally, we observe stark differences in statistical efficiency and consistency by varying the number of in-context examples and task difficulty. We also measure each architecture's predisposition towards in-context learning when presented with the option to memorize rather than leverage in-context examples. Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, we find that several attention alternatives are sometimes competitive with or better in-context learners than transformers. However, no single architecture demonstrates consistency across all tasks, with performance either plateauing or declining when confronted with a significantly larger number of in-context examples than those encountered during gradient-based training.

papers.title: Attention with Markov: A Framework for Principled Analysis of Transformers via Markov Chains
papers.research_question: Can we systematically characterize the learning capabilities of single-layer transformers with Markovian inputs, specifically their loss landscape and why they sometimes fail to learn the Markov kernel?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for principled analysis of transformers via Markov chains and theoretically characterizes the loss landscape of single-layer transformers, showing the existence of global minima (bigram) and bad local minima (unigram) depending on data properties and weight tying.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a novel framework for systematic theoretical and empirical study of transformers via Markov chains, characterizing the loss landscape and revealing insights about the learning capabilities of single-layer and deeper transformers.
papers.key_findings:
