Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Beyond Human-Like Processing: Large Language Models Perform Equivalently on Forward and Backward Scientific Text
papers.research_question: Does the success of large language models arise from their flexibility as general pattern learners, rather than from human-like language processing mechanisms? This is investigated by training LLMs on forward and backward scientific text.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer-based LLMs perform equally well on forward and backward scientific text, suggesting they are general pattern learning machines rather than models of human language processing.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based language models are best understood as general pattern learning machines capable of extracting predictive structure from any sufficiently structured input, rather than as specific models of human language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Backward-trained GPT-2 models performed non-significantly better than forward-trained models on the BrainBench task.
Both forward and backward-trained models matched or exceeded human expert performance as model size increased.
Backward-trained models exhibited consistently higher perplexities on validation and test data.
Backward-trained models showed lower correlation with human judgments compared to forward-trained models.
Model judgments correlated more strongly with each other than with human judgments.
papers.abstract: The impressive performance of large language models (LLMs) has led to their consideration as models of human language processing. Instead, we suggest that the success of LLMs arises from the flexibility of the transformer learning architecture. To evaluate this conjecture, we trained LLMs on scientific texts that were either in a forward or backward format. Despite backward text being inconsistent with the structure of human languages, we found that LLMs performed equally well in either format on a neuroscience benchmark, eclipsing human expert performance for both forward and backward orders. Our results are consistent with the success of transformers across diverse domains, such as weather prediction and protein design. This widespread success is attributable to LLM's ability to extract predictive patterns from any sufficiently structured input. Given their generality, we suggest caution in interpreting LLM's success in linguistic tasks as evidence for human-like mechanisms.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Interpreting Evo 2: Arc Institute's Next-Generation Genomic Foundation Model
papers.research_question: How can interpretability techniques be applied to the Evo 2 genomic foundation model to extract biologically relevant features and enable steering for DNA sequence generation?
papers.core_contribution: Applied interpretability techniques to Evo 2 to extract biologically relevant features and demonstrated potential for steering DNA sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability methods applied to Evo 2 reveal biological knowledge and open possibilities for genome engineering and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered features corresponding to biological concepts like coding sequences, protein secondary structure, tRNA/rRNAs, and viral derived sequences.
Validated feature relevance with domain-F1 score alignment analysis.
Found that layer 26 (StripedHyena layer) had the most interesting biologically-relevant features.
Early indications that steering through features could enable controlled DNA sequence generation.
BatchTopK SAEs performed better than standard ReLU SAEs in training loss and feature crispness.
papers.limitation:
Steering is more complex than for language models and requires further research
Work is in early stages
future_direction: Publishing a comprehensive study on interpretability methodology
Unlocking steering capabilities for DNA sequence generation
papers.abstract: How can interpretability techniques be applied to the Evo 2 genomic foundation model to extract biologically relevant features and enable steering for DNA sequence generation? Applied interpretability techniques to Evo 2 to extract biologically relevant features and demonstrated potential for steering DNA sequence generation. Interpretability methods applied to Evo 2 reveal biological knowledge and open possibilities for genome engineering and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Beyond performance: How design choices shape chemical language models
papers.research_question: How do design choices (molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, model architecture) influence the performance and chemical interpretability of chemical language models?
papers.core_contribution: Design choices, particularly molecular representation and tokenization, significantly affect the chemical interpretability of language models, with SMILES and atomwise tokenization yielding more chemically meaningful embeddings, even when downstream task performance is similar.
papers.conclusion: Design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented in language models, and SMILES with atomwise tokenization is favorable for interpretability, guiding future development of chemically grounded CLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Atomwise tokenization generally yields better downstream performance than SentencePiece tokenization.
SMILES representations produce more chemically structured latent spaces than SELFIES representations.
BART and RoBERTa architectures yield comparably interpretable representations, but BART embeddings are more linearly separable for certain molecular properties.
RoBERTa shows a stronger ability to distinguish between atom types than BART.
The choice of molecular representation has a greater impact on interpretability than the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring alternative molecular representations such as t-SMILES and DeepSMILES.
Comparing BART's generative capabilities with other large language model architectures like GPT.
Investigating the differences and synergies between large language models and graph-based approaches such as GROVER.
Utilizing highly curated datasets from specialized domains to reveal subtle chemical relationships.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical language models (CLMs) have shown strong performance in molecular property prediction and generation tasks. However, the impact of design choices, such as molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, and model architecture, on both performance and chemical interpretability remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate how these factors influence CLM performance and chemical understanding. We evaluated models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks and probing the structure of their latent spaces using simple classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques.Despite similar performance on downstream tasks across model configurations, we observed substantial differences in the structure and interpretability of their internal representations. SMILES molecular representation format with atomwise tokenization strategy consistently produced more chemically meaningful embeddings, while models based on BART and RoBERTa architectures yielded comparably interpretable representations. These findings highlight that design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented, even when external metrics appear unchanged. This insight can inform future model development, encouraging more chemically grounded and interpretable CLMs.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Analyzing Encoded Concepts in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether transformer language models encode linguistic concepts in their representations, which concepts dominate the overall structure, and whether the models learn novel concepts beyond linguistic properties.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ConceptX, a framework that uses unsupervised clustering to discover latent concepts in transformer language model representations and aligns them with human-defined concepts to explain how linguistic knowledge is structured across layers and models.
papers.conclusion: ConceptX provides a framework for analyzing encoded concepts in deep NLP models, revealing how linguistic information is structured across layers and highlighting differences between models, with many concepts being compositional or novel.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of transformer models predominantly capture shallow lexical concepts (e.g., ngrams, suffixes), while middle and higher layers better represent core linguistic concepts (e.g., morphology, syntax, semantics).
Multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R) show higher alignment with human-defined concepts compared to monolingual models, likely due to more complex training tasks.
Roughly 50% of the encoded concepts discovered align with the suite of human-defined linguistic concepts; the remaining concepts are novel or compositional, involving multiple fine-grained categories.
The extent of alignment varies across different transformer models and different human-defined concepts, influenced by factors like architecture, training data, and objective function.
Models learn multi-faceted concepts that cannot be adequately explained by existing human-defined concepts, indicating the presence of novel semantic relationships.
papers.limitation:
Clustering a large number of high-dimensional vectors is computationally and memory intensive, requiring the use of a subset of data and limiting the number of tokens per word.
The number of clusters (K=1000) was selected empirically rather than through a rigorous optimization method.
papers.abstract: We propose a novel framework ConceptX, to analyze how latent concepts are encoded in representations learned within pre-trained language models. It uses clustering to discover the encoded concepts and explains them by aligning with a large set of human-defined concepts. Our analysis on seven transformer language models reveal interesting insights: i) the latent space within the learned representations overlap with different linguistic concepts to a varying degree, ii) the lower layers in the model are dominated by lexical concepts (e.g., affixation), whereas the core-linguistic concepts (e.g., morphological or syntactic relations) are better represented in the middle and higher layers, iii) some encoded concepts are multi-faceted and cannot be adequately explained using the existing human-defined concepts.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Is attention required for ICL? Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between model architecture and in-context learning ability? Which architectures are capable of ICL and which exhibit superior performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that in-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with some attention alternatives being competitive with or better than transformers in certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with attention alternatives being competitive. However, no architecture is consistent across all tasks, and performance degrades with out-of-distribution prompt lengths.
papers.key_findings:
All considered architectures can perform in-context learning, demonstrating ICL is not exclusive to attention-based models.
Attention alternatives such as Mamba, Hyena, RetNet, and RWKV are sometimes competitive with or better than transformers at ICL.
Performance varies with number of in-context examples; some architectures show degradation when extrapolating to longer prompts than seen in training.
The emergence of ICL in image classification is influenced by burstiness in training data; some architectures are predisposed towards memorization over ICL.
ICL score in language modeling correlates with performance on other ICL tasks, but not perfectly.
papers.abstract: What is the relationship between model architecture and the ability to perform in-context learning? In this empirical study, we take the first steps toward answering this question. We evaluate thirteen model architectures capable of causal language modeling across a suite of synthetic in-context learning tasks. These selected architectures represent a broad range of paradigms, including recurrent and convolution-based neural networks, transformers, state space model inspired, and other emerging attention alternatives. We discover that all the considered architectures can perform in-context learning under a wider range of conditions than previously documented. Additionally, we observe stark differences in statistical efficiency and consistency by varying the number of in-context examples and task difficulty. We also measure each architecture's predisposition towards in-context learning when presented with the option to memorize rather than leverage in-context examples. Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, we find that several attention alternatives are sometimes competitive with or better in-context learners than transformers. However, no single architecture demonstrates consistency across all tasks, with performance either plateauing or declining when confronted with a significantly larger number of in-context examples than those encountered during gradient-based training.

papers.title: Attention with Markov: A Framework for Principled Analysis of Transformers via Markov Chains
papers.research_question: Can we systematically characterize the learning capabilities of single-layer transformers with Markovian inputs, specifically their loss landscape and why they sometimes fail to learn the Markov kernel?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for principled analysis of transformers via Markov chains and theoretically characterizes the loss landscape of single-layer transformers, showing the existence of global minima (bigram) and bad local minima (unigram) depending on data properties and weight tying.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a novel framework for systematic theoretical and empirical study of transformers via Markov chains, characterizing the loss landscape and revealing insights about the learning capabilities of single-layer and deeper transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer transformers with weight tying can get stuck in bad local minima corresponding to the unigram distribution when trained on first-order Markov chains with switching factor p+q > 1.
Removing weight tying turns these bad local minima into saddle points, allowing convergence to the global minima (bigram) for p+q > 1.
For switching factor p+q < 1, single-layer transformers converge to the global minima regardless of weight tying.
Transformers with two or more layers always converge to the global minima irrespective of switching factor and weight tying.
The presence of local optima is influenced by the Markov switching probabilities and the transformer's weight-tying, revealing an interplay between data distribution, architecture, and performance.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to first-order binary Markov chains and single-layer transformers, with open questions for higher-order chains and deeper models.
future_direction: Establishing similar results for higher-order Markov chains.
Extending the analysis to deeper transformer models.
papers.abstract: In recent years, attention-based transformers have achieved tremendous success across a variety of disciplines including natural languages. A key ingredient behind their success is the generative pretraining procedure, during which these models are trained on a large text corpus in an auto-regressive manner. To shed light on this phenomenon, we propose a new framework that allows both theory and systematic experiments to study the sequential modeling capabilities of transformers through the lens of Markov chains. Inspired by the Markovianity of natural languages, we model the data as a Markovian source and utilize this framework to systematically study the interplay between the data-distributional properties, the transformer architecture, the learnt distribution, and the final model performance. In particular, we theoretically characterize the loss landscape of single-layer transformers and show the existence of global minima and bad local minima contingent upon the specific data characteristics and the transformer architecture. Backed by experiments, we demonstrate that our theoretical findings are in congruence with the empirical results. We further investigate these findings in the broader context of higher order Markov chains and deeper architectures, and outline open problems in this arena. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Bond1995/Markov}.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Interpreting Affine Recurrence Learning in GPT-style Transformers
papers.research_question: How do GPT-style transformers internally learn and predict affine recurrences as an in-context learning task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that a custom transformer learns affine recurrences by forming an initial estimate via a copying mechanism in the zeroth layer, which is then refined by negative similarity heads in the second layer.
papers.conclusion: The study provides empirical and theoretical evidence that GPT-style transformers solve affine recurrences through a two-stage process: an initial estimate in the zeroth layer and refinement via negative similarity heads in the second layer.
papers.key_findings:
The zeroth layer attention heads act as 'previous token heads', copying the previous vector and adding information to the orthogonal complement of the embedding space.
The first layer heads are less useful and act primarily as bias terms, with minimal input-dependent contribution.
The second layer heads function as 'negative similarity heads', with QK circuits approximating identity and OV circuits as negative identity, correcting the initial overestimate.
The model's mechanism involves a zeroth layer that provides a crude shape-correcting estimate, followed by a second layer that refines this estimate.
Analysis of the OV circuits in layer 0 shows a linear relationship with the residual stream vectors, indicating a copying mechanism with a specific scaling factor.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to higher-dimensional linear recurrences.
Exploring polynomial recurrences within transformers.
Conducting more fine-grained analysis of how transformers complete the affine recurrence task.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of GPT-style transformers, particularly their capacity to perform in-context learning (ICL), is critical for advancing AI alignment and interpretability. In-context learning allows transformers to generalize during inference without modifying their weights, yet the precise operations driving this capability remain largely opaque. This paper presents an investigation into the mechanistic interpretability of these transformers, focusing specifically on their ability to learn and predict affine recurrences as an ICL task. To address this, we trained a custom three-layer transformer to predict affine recurrences and analyzed the model's internal operations using both empirical and theoretical approaches. Our findings reveal that the model forms an initial estimate of the target sequence using a copying mechanism in the zeroth layer, which is subsequently refined through negative similarity heads in the second layer. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of transformer behaviors in recursive tasks and offer potential avenues for improving AI alignment through mechanistic interpretability. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for future work, including extensions to higher-dimensional recurrences and the exploration of polynomial sequences.

papers.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Why does in-context learning (ICL) emerge and then disappear (transience) during training, and what are the dynamics between ICL and other learning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The transience of in-context learning (ICL) is explained by coopetition (cooperative and competitive dynamics) between ICL and a newly identified strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), where shared sub-circuits enable ICL emergence before CIWL asymptotically dominates.
papers.conclusion: Strategy coopetition between ICL and CIWL explains the emergence and transience of ICL, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of how capabilities dynamically trade off during transformer training.
papers.key_findings:
The asymptotic strategy after ICL transience is a hybrid called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), which depends on both in-weights information and the presence of the correct label in context.
ICL and CIWL share critical sub-circuits (e.g., Layer 2 induction heads), leading to cooperative dynamics that enable ICL emergence.
ICL emergence is only possible when CIWL is not fully formed, and ICL is faster to emerge but asymptotically dominated by CIWL.
A minimal mathematical model captures the coopetition dynamics and explains transience.
Matching context and query exemplars in the data can make ICL persistent by removing the asymptotic bias towards CIWL.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that, after the disappearance of ICL, the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term "context-constrained in-weights learning" (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term "strategy coopetition." We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Hierarchical Transformers Are More Efficient Language Models
papers.research_question: Does having an explicit hierarchical architecture lead to more efficient Transformers for handling long sequences?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hourglass, a hierarchical Transformer architecture that uses shortening and upsampling to improve computational efficiency and performance in language modeling and image generation tasks.
papers.conclusion: Hierarchical Transformers, as instantiated by the Hourglass architecture, are more efficient and achieve competitive results on language modeling and image generation tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Hourglass improves perplexity and reduces computational cost compared to Transformer-XL and Reformer baselines on the enwik8 dataset.
Hourglass achieves state-of-the-art results among autoregressive Transformer models on the ImageNet32 image generation task (3.741 bpd).
The proposed shorten factor dropout training technique improves validation loss compared to training with a fixed shorten factor.
Hourglass can be used with any attention type (e.g., relative attention, LSH attention) and shows efficiency gains across modalities.
future_direction: Using Hourglass with other attention types for processing longer sequences.
Advancing the shortening mechanism, e.g., dynamic pooling to handle fixed-size groups in multi-stage shortening.
Investigating the best hierarchy for a given task, especially with longer contexts.
papers.abstract: Transformer models yield impressive results on many NLP and sequence modeling tasks. Remarkably, Transformers can handle long sequences, which allows them to produce long coherent outputs: entire paragraphs produced by GPT-3 or well-structured images produced by DALL-E. These large language models are impressive but also very inefficient and costly, which limits their applications and accessibility. We postulate that having an explicit hierarchical architecture is the key to Transformers that efficiently handle long sequences. To verify this claim, we first study different ways to downsample and upsample activations in Transformers so as to make them hierarchical. We use the best performing upsampling and downsampling layers to create Hourglass -a hierarchical Transformer language model. Hourglass improves upon the Transformer baseline given the same amount of computation and can yield the same results as Transformers more efficiently. In particular, Hourglass sets new state-of-the-art for Transformer models on the ImageNet32 generation task and improves language modeling efficiency on the widely studied enwik8 benchmark.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Secretly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning in GPT models? The paper investigates whether in-context learning can be understood as a form of implicit finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning by showing a dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, and provides empirical evidence that ICL behaves similarly to explicit finetuning.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be understood as a process of meta-optimization, specifically as implicit finetuning, and this understanding can inspire improved model designs like momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent.
In-context learning updates attention outputs and weights in a direction similar to explicit finetuning.
In-context learning covers most of the correct predictions made by a finetuned model.
In-context learning and finetuning pay similar attention to training tokens.
A momentum-based attention mechanism, inspired by the dual form, improves performance over vanilla attention in language modeling and ICL tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based architectures and does not cover other architectures like LSTMs.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard Transformer attention may be more complex.
Due to computational cost, the analysis is limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and does not include larger models.
The analysis is based only on classification tasks and does not consider other task types like multiple choice or open-ended generation.
future_direction: Study in-context learning in non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models (e.g., GPT 13B).
Investigate in-context learning on other task types like multiple choice and open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at https://aka.ms/icl.

papers.title: Selective Induction Heads: How Transformers Select Causal Structures In Context
papers.research_question: How do transformers select causal structures in context? Specifically, how can they dynamically handle causal structures that change with context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for selective induction heads, showing how transformers can learn to select the correct causal structure in-context for next-token prediction in interleaved Markov chains.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn selective induction heads to dynamically select the correct causal structure in-context.
A 3-layer attention-only transformer can implement the selective induction head mechanism.
The constructed transformer matches the performance of trained transformers.
The mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution.
papers.abstract: Transformers have exhibited exceptional capabilities in sequence modeling tasks, leveraging self-attention and in-context learning. Critical to this success are induction heads, attention circuits that enable copying tokens based on their previous occurrences. In this work, we introduce a novel framework that showcases transformers' ability to dynamically handle causal structures. Existing works rely on Markov Chains to study the formation of induction heads, revealing how transformers capture causal dependencies and learn transition probabilities in-context. However, they rely on a fixed causal structure that fails to capture the complexity of natural languages, where the relationship between tokens dynamically changes with context. To this end, our framework varies the causal structure through interleaved Markov chains with different lags while keeping the transition probabilities fixed. This setting unveils the formation of Selective Induction Heads, a new circuit that endows transformers with the ability to select the correct causal structure in-context. We empirically demonstrate that transformers learn this mechanism to predict the next token by identifying the correct lag and copying the corresponding token from the past. We provide a detailed construction of a 3-layer transformer to implement the selective induction head, and a theoretical analysis proving that this mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution. Our findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Tracr-Injection: Distilling Algorithms into Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we distill algorithms written in RASP into a pre-trained language model to enhance symbolic capabilities and provide interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces tracr-injection, a method to distill algorithms written in RASP into a pre-trained language model, creating an interpretable subspace in the residual stream and improving out-of-distribution generalization for some tasks.
papers.conclusion: Tracr-injection provides a first step towards injecting ground truth mechanisms into pre-trained language models, offering interpretable representations and potential for benchmarking interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully distills three algorithms (Shuffle-Dyck, counting, integer addition) into GPT-2-large, achieving high accuracy on the injected tasks.
The method creates an interpretable subspace in the residual stream that can be decoded into the RASP variables of the compiled algorithm.
Noise perturbation experiments show the injected symbolic representations are causally used by the model for predictions.
For some tasks (e.g., Shuffle-Dyck), the method improves out-of-distribution generalization compared to a standard finetuning baseline.
The method does not induce catastrophic forgetting, maintaining performance on unrelated language modeling and classification tasks.
papers.limitation:
The model does not generalize well to out-of-distribution examples that are radically different from the training distribution.
The method is demonstrated on only three simple symbolic tasks.
The evaluation is limited to GPT-2, and scaling to larger models is left for future work.
future_direction: Understanding why certain injected algorithms (e.g., Shuffle-Dyck) generalize better out-of-distribution than others.
Scaling the method to more complex tasks and RASP programs.
Using the method to benchmark automated circuit discovery and other interpretability techniques.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the surge of large language models, there has been a push to formally characterize the symbolic abilities intrinsic to the transformer architecture. A programming language, called RASP, has been proposed, which can be directly compiled into transformer weights to implement these algorithms. However, the tasks that can be implemented in RASP are often uncommon to learn from natural unsupervised data, showing a mismatch between theoretical capabilities of the transformer architecture, and the practical learnability of these capabilities from unsupervised data. We propose tracr-injection, a method that allows us to distill algorithms written in RASP directly into a pre-trained language model. We showcase our method by injecting 3 different algorithms into a language model. We show how our method creates an interpretable subspace within the model's residual stream, which can be decoded into the variables present in the code of the RASP algorithm. Additionally, we found that the proposed method can improve out-of-distribution performance compared to our baseline, indicating that indeed a more symbolic mechanism is taking place in the inner workings of the model. We release the code used to run our experiments.

papers.title: Learning a Fourier Transform for Linear Relative Positional Encodings in Transformers
papers.research_question: How to efficiently incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs) into linear Transformers, enabling linear complexity for both sequential and geometric data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), a class of linear Transformers that efficiently incorporate relative positional encodings (RPEs) by learning their spectral representation, achieving linear complexity and applicability to sequential and geometric data.
papers.conclusion: FLTs provide an efficient and effective method for incorporating RPEs into linear attention Transformers, with theoretical approximation guarantees and strong empirical performance across text, image, and 3D molecular data.
papers.key_findings:
FLTs outperform other linear Transformers (e.g., Performer, CosFormer) on language modeling (WikiText-103) by achieving lower perplexity.
FLTs achieve higher accuracy than baselines on image classification tasks (ImageNet, Places365, Fashion-MNIST).
For 3D molecular property prediction (OC20 dataset), FLTs with RPEs provide better energy prediction accuracy (lower MAE, higher EwT) than Performers without RPEs.
FLTs maintain linear time and space complexity, being more memory-efficient than log-linear Performer baselines.
FLTs can learn local RPEs and exhibit both local and global attention patterns in language modeling.
papers.abstract: We propose a new class of linear Transformers called FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), which incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs). These include regular RPE techniques applied for sequential data, as well as novel RPEs operating on geometric data embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. FLTs construct the optimal RPE mechanism implicitly by learning its spectral representation. As opposed to other architectures combining efficient low-rank linear attention with RPEs, FLTs remain practical in terms of their memory usage and do not require additional assumptions about the structure of the RPE mask. Besides, FLTs allow for applying certain structural inductive bias techniques to specify masking strategies, e.g. they provide a way to learn the so-called local RPEs introduced in this paper and give accuracy gains as compared with several other linear Transformers for language modeling. We also thoroughly test FLTs on other data modalities and tasks, such as image classification, 3D molecular modeling, and learnable optimizers. To the best of our knowledge, for 3D molecular data, FLTs are the first Transformer architectures providing linear attention and incorporating RPE masking.

papers.title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning emerge in autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction? The paper investigates whether such training gives rise to a gradient-based optimization algorithm (mesa-optimizer) that adjusts the model as new inputs are revealed.
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn a gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithm that performs in-context learning, explaining the emergence of in-context learning and inspiring new Transformer layers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in autoregressive Transformers arises from mesa-optimization algorithms learned during training, which can be leveraged to design more efficient optimization-based layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early Transformer layers learn a token binding mechanism that aggregates consecutive observations into internal representations, enabling subsequent mesa-optimization.
Trained single-layer linear self-attention models implement one-step gradient descent on a least-squares objective, matching the theoretical construction.
Multi-layer linear self-attention models implement a preconditioned gradient descent algorithm that approximates the optimal least-squares solution.
The proposed mesa-layer, derived from optimization principles, performs recursive least squares and improves language modeling performance compared to standard linear attention.
Standard softmax Transformers trained on synthetic sequence tasks exhibit internal activation patterns consistent with mesa-optimization across layers.
papers.limitation: The language modeling results are not sufficient to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers; more reverse-engineering is needed.
future_direction: Studying the mesa-layer equipped with forgetting factors
More reverse-engineering work to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers
Designing new optimization-based Transformer layers
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant model in deep learning, but the reason for their superior performance is poorly understood. Here, we hypothesize that the strong performance of Transformers stems from an architectural bias towards mesa-optimization, a learned process running within the forward pass of a model consisting of the following two steps: (i) the construction of an internal learning objective, and (ii) its corresponding solution found through optimization. To test this hypothesis, we reverse-engineer a series of autoregressive Transformers trained on simple sequence modeling tasks, uncovering underlying gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithms driving the generation of predictions. Moreover, we show that the learned forward-pass optimization algorithm can be immediately repurposed to solve supervised few-shot tasks, suggesting that mesa-optimization might underlie the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Finally, we propose a novel self-attention layer, the mesa-layer, that explicitly and efficiently solves optimization problems specified in context. We find that this layer can lead to improved performance in synthetic and preliminary language modeling experiments, adding weight to our hypothesis that mesa-optimization is an important operation hidden within the weights of trained Transformers.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Emergent Stack Representations in Modeling Counter Languages Using Transformers
papers.research_question: Do transformer models trained as next token predictors on counter languages learn internal representations that mimic stack structures?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained as next token predictors on counter languages learn internal representations that encode stack depth, indicating they develop stack-like structures.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on counter languages learn internal representations that mimic stack structures, providing insights into how they process such languages and aiding in circuit discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Probing classifiers achieve high accuracy in predicting stack depth from internal representations, indicating that transformers learn stack-like representations.
The difference between task accuracy and control task accuracy (selectivity) is high, indicating that the probes are not learning spurious correlations.
Probing accuracy is higher for Shuffle languages with more stacks, which is attributed to lower update frequency per stack.
The same probing setup successfully recovers stack depth in a Tracr-compiled model, validating the probing methodology.
papers.limitation: Probing classifiers do not provide causal information about the features they detect.
future_direction: Determine the causal role of the stack-like structures in model computations.
Explore how the stack structures are updated and read out by the model's algorithm.
Use more robust mechanistic interpretability techniques to confirm and extend findings.
papers.abstract: Transformer architectures are the backbone of most modern language models, but understanding the inner workings of these models still largely remains an open problem.
